author: A Robot
objectives: Identify DNA structural components: sugar-phosphate backbones, adenine, thymine, guanine, cytosine, and hydrogen bonds between base pairs.
Apply complementary base-pairing rules and relate A-T and G-C pairings to two versus three hydrogen bonds.
Explain antiparallel 5'-to-3' strand orientation as a consequence of sugar-phosphate backbone chemistry.
Trace the functions of helicase, single-strand binding proteins, DNA polymerase, and DNA ligase at the replication fork.
Explain why leading-strand synthesis is continuous while lagging-strand synthesis occurs as Okazaki fragments.
Predict DNA molecule composition after one and two rounds of semiconservative replication.

modules.moduleName: Scene 1: DNA as a Schematic Ladder
modules.description: A flat DNA ladder model introduces the two sugar-phosphate backbones, inward-projecting bases, and complementary rungs before helical geometry is added.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the sugar-phosphate backbones as the outside rails of DNA.
Identify the four nitrogenous bases by one-letter labels and color coding.
Describe base pairs as rungs held together by hydrogen bonds.
instructions: View the ladder from the front of the tabletop workspace.
Advance through the clips to reveal backbones, bases, and hydrogen-bond markers.
Use the labels to connect the schematic shapes to DNA vocabulary.

components.text: Bases: A = adenine, T = thymine, G = guanine, C = cytosine
DNA ladder model: backbones outside, bases inside

clips.changeMeaning: The schematic DNA ladder is placed in the center of the workspace to establish a simple structural representation before molecular details are highlighted.
clips.narration: We begin with DNA as a flat ladder. The outside rails represent sugar-phosphate backbones, and the horizontal rungs represent paired nitrogenous bases.

components.text: Sugar-phosphate backbones form the two outside rails

clips.changeMeaning: Backbone highlight strips appear on both outside rails so students distinguish the repeating sugar-phosphate scaffold from the base-pair rungs.
clips.narration: Each rail is a repeating sugar-phosphate backbone. The bases attach to sugars and point inward toward bases on the opposite strand.

components.text: Base pairs are held by hydrogen bonds across the center

clips.changeMeaning: The base identity panel and dashed bond markers appear, connecting the color-coded rungs to base names and introducing hydrogen bonds between paired bases.
clips.narration: The bases are adenine, thymine, guanine, and cytosine. Paired bases meet in the center, where dashed lines represent hydrogen bonds.

modules.description: The schematic ladder is compared with a three-dimensional double helix so students map rails to spiraling backbones and rungs to stacked base pairs.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Map a flat DNA ladder representation onto the double helix.
Describe backbones as two spirals around a common axis.
State that B-form DNA completes about one turn every ten base pairs.
instructions: Compare the schematic model on the left with the helical model on the right.
Use the representation cue to mentally switch between ladder and helix.
Observe the helical grooves as geometric features of real DNA.

components.text: ~10 base pairs per full helical turn
The same DNA can be viewed as a ladder or as a helix

clips.changeMeaning: The previous ladder remains visible as a reference point, supporting continuity between the introductory schematic and the upcoming realistic geometry.
clips.narration: The ladder drawing is a useful simplification. Now we will map that flat drawing onto the three-dimensional shape of DNA.

components.text: Backbones spiral outside; base pairs stack inside

clips.changeMeaning: The double helix appears beside the ladder, allowing students to compare rails with spiraling backbones and rungs with stacked internal base pairs.
clips.narration: In real DNA, the two sugar-phosphate backbones spiral around a common axis. The base pairs stack inside the helix. One full turn contains about ten base pairs.

components.text: Major and minor grooves are visible features of the 3D helix

clips.changeMeaning: The helix is enlarged slightly and the cue text emphasizes observable grooves, keeping attention on geometric mapping without introducing groove function.
clips.narration: The twisting geometry creates major and minor grooves that you can see. For this lab, focus on how the same paired bases and backbones are arranged in three dimensions.

modules.description: Direction arrows and termini labels appear on the double helix to explain antiparallel strand orientation and 5'-to-3' backbone directionality.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the 5' and 3' termini on both DNA strands.
Explain that complementary DNA strands run in opposite directions.
Relate antiparallel arrangement to directional sugar-phosphate backbone chemistry.
instructions: Follow the red arrow on one backbone and the blue arrow on the other.
Compare the location of each 5' and 3' label.
Move around the model to confirm that the arrows point in opposite directions.

components.text: Antiparallel: one strand runs 5'→3', the other runs 3'→5'

clips.changeMeaning: The helix appears without arrows first, preserving continuity with the previous scene while preparing students for a new directional overlay.
clips.narration: Each DNA strand has a chemical direction, described using 5 prime and 3 prime ends of the sugar-phosphate backbone.

clips.changeMeaning: A red 5' to 3' arrow and termini labels appear on one backbone, showing that one strand has a defined chemical orientation.
clips.narration: This red arrow traces one strand from its 5 prime end to its 3 prime end. The labels refer to carbon positions in the sugar ring at the backbone ends.

clips.changeMeaning: A blue arrow appears on the complementary backbone pointing the opposite way, making antiparallel orientation visually explicit.
clips.narration: The other strand runs in the opposite direction. DNA strands are antiparallel: if one strand goes 5 prime to 3 prime upward, the complementary strand goes 5 prime to 3 prime downward.

modules.description: Students complete a missing complementary strand from a base palette; correct pairs snap into place and display two or three hydrogen bonds.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Apply A-T and G-C base-pairing rules to construct a complementary strand.
Differentiate A-T pairs with two hydrogen bonds from G-C pairs with three hydrogen bonds.
Determine the antiparallel orientation of the completed complementary sequence.
instructions: Use the four loose base tokens as the base palette.
Place the correct complement across from each template base.
Correct answers reveal hydrogen-bond lines; incorrect choices are rejected by the activity prefab.

components.text: Template: 5'-ATGCCAGT-3'. Build the complement.

clips.changeMeaning: The template strand, empty complementary backbone, and four draggable base prefabs are staged as a structured base-pairing puzzle.
clips.narration: Use the template sequence five prime A T G C C A G T three prime to build the complementary strand. Choose each base according to complementarity.

components.text: A pairs with T; G pairs with C. Correct pairs snap in and show bonds.

clips.changeMeaning: The instruction panel changes to state the complementary rules and describes how correct and incorrect placements will behave.
clips.narration: A pairs with T, and G pairs with C. Correct placements snap into position. Incorrect placements are rejected because the hydrogen-bonding patterns do not match.

components.text: Complement: 3'-TACGGTCA-5'. A-T = 2 H bonds; G-C = 3.

clips.changeMeaning: The completed complement and hydrogen-bond overlay appear so students can verify sequence, antiparallel orientation, and bond counts.
clips.narration: The correct complement is three prime T A C G G T C A five prime. A-T base pairs have two hydrogen bonds, while G-C base pairs have three.

modules.moduleName: Scene 5: Helicase Opens the Replication Fork
modules.description: Helicase appears at one end of a DNA double helix and moves forward, converting closed DNA into a Y-shaped replication fork with exposed bases.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify helicase as the enzyme that opens the DNA double helix.
Describe the replication fork as the Y-shaped region where parental strands separate.
Explain that helicase disrupts hydrogen bonds between paired bases.
instructions: Watch helicase move along the DNA segment.
Observe closed paired DNA changing into separated template strands.
Identify the Y-shaped replication fork after unwinding.

components.text: Helicase
Replication fork: parental strands separate here

clips.changeMeaning: Helicase is positioned at the left end of a closed DNA segment, introducing the enzyme before the unwinding transformation occurs.
clips.narration: Replication begins when helicase binds DNA and moves along the double helix. Its job is to open the molecule so each strand can serve as a template.

clips.changeMeaning: Helicase moves toward the center and the closed helix is replaced by an opened fork model, showing separation of the parental strands.
clips.narration: As helicase advances, it disrupts hydrogen bonds between base pairs. Behind it, the parental strands separate into a Y-shaped replication fork.

components.text: Exposed bases can now guide complementary synthesis

clips.changeMeaning: The opened fork is enlarged and the label changes to emphasize the biological significance of exposed bases as templates for new strand synthesis.
clips.narration: The exposed bases now contain the information needed to build complementary strands. But single-stranded DNA must be stabilized before copying continues.

modules.moduleName: Scene 6: Single-Strand Binding Proteins Stabilize DNA
modules.description: Single-strand binding proteins attach to the separated templates behind helicase and prevent strands from re-pairing or folding on themselves.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify SSB proteins bound along exposed single-stranded DNA.
Explain why separated DNA strands are unstable without SSBs.
Describe SSBs as keeping template strands open and accessible.
instructions: Compare the unstable open fork with the stabilized fork.
Notice where the blue SSB spheres bind along both exposed strands.
Advance to see how SSBs prevent collapse of the separated templates.

components.text: Single strands must be held open for copying
SSB proteins

clips.changeMeaning: An opened replication fork is shown without stabilizing proteins to focus attention on the instability of exposed single-stranded DNA.
clips.narration: Once DNA is opened, the separated strands are not naturally stable. They can re-pair with each other or fold into shapes that block copying.

components.text: Without help, exposed strands tend to re-pair or fold

clips.changeMeaning: A collapse preview appears over the fork to visualize the tendency of single strands to reanneal or form secondary structures.
clips.narration: This preview shows the problem. Complementary regions can reanneal, and single strands can fold back on themselves.

components.text: SSBs stabilize templates and keep bases accessible

clips.changeMeaning: SSB clusters appear on both exposed strands and the collapse preview disappears, showing stabilization of template DNA behind helicase.
clips.narration: Single-strand binding proteins, or SSBs, bind the exposed templates. They keep the strands open and accessible for DNA polymerase.

modules.description: DNA polymerase copies the template oriented for continuous synthesis, adding nucleotides to a primer and following the replication fork.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain that DNA polymerase extends DNA only by adding nucleotides to a 3' end.
Identify the leading strand as the continuously synthesized new strand.
Relate continuous leading-strand synthesis to polymerase movement with the replication fork.
instructions: Locate the primer and polymerase on the upper template.
Watch free nucleotides appear and the new strand extend.
Compare polymerase movement with the direction of fork opening.

components.text: DNA polymerase builds new DNA 5'→3'

clips.changeMeaning: DNA polymerase and a primer segment are shown on the leading-strand template, introducing the need for a 3' end to extend.
clips.narration: DNA polymerase cannot start from nothing; it extends from a primer. It adds each incoming nucleotide to the 3 prime end, so new DNA is built 5 prime to 3 prime.

components.text: Free nucleotides pair with exposed template bases

clips.changeMeaning: Free nucleotide substrates appear near the fork to show the raw materials that pair with exposed template bases before being linked by polymerase.
clips.narration: Free nucleotides diffuse in, pair with their complementary template bases, and are covalently joined into the growing strand by polymerase.

components.text: Leading strand: continuous synthesis toward the fork

clips.changeMeaning: The polymerase moves toward the fork and the new leading strand grows longer, demonstrating continuous synthesis in the same direction as fork movement.
clips.narration: On this template, polymerase can move with the fork while synthesizing 5 prime to 3 prime. The result is a continuously synthesized leading strand.

modules.moduleName: Scene 8: Lagging-Strand Synthesis and Okazaki Fragments
modules.description: The opposite template is copied in short Okazaki fragments because polymerase must synthesize 5' to 3' away from the fork; ligase seals the fragments.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain why lagging-strand synthesis is discontinuous on the opposite antiparallel template.
Identify Okazaki fragments as short DNA segments synthesized 5' to 3'.
Describe DNA ligase as sealing nicks between Okazaki fragments.
instructions: Watch polymerase synthesize a short fragment away from the fork.
Observe repeated fragment formation as polymerase returns near the fork.
Advance to see ligase convert fragments into a continuous strand.

components.text: Lagging strand: short 5'→3' fragments

clips.changeMeaning: The lagging template is staged with polymerase near the fork to introduce the directional conflict caused by antiparallel template orientation.
clips.narration: On the other template, polymerase cannot follow the fork continuously because it still must synthesize the new strand 5 prime to 3 prime.

components.text: Fragment 1 grows away from the fork

clips.changeMeaning: Polymerase moves away from the fork and the first Okazaki fragment appears, showing that each fragment grows in the permitted 5' to 3' direction.
clips.narration: Polymerase starts near the fork but works away from it, creating a short DNA segment called an Okazaki fragment.

components.text: Polymerase repeatedly jumps back to begin new fragments

clips.changeMeaning: Two more Okazaki fragments appear at staggered positions, demonstrating repeated restart events on the lagging strand template.
clips.narration: As helicase exposes more template, polymerase repeatedly returns near the fork and makes another fragment. This is discontinuous lagging-strand synthesis.

components.text: DNA ligase seals nicks to make a continuous strand

clips.changeMeaning: Ligase appears and the separate fragments are replaced by a continuous strand, making the sealing of nicks between fragments visible.
clips.narration: DNA ligase seals the nicks between Okazaki fragments, converting the discontinuous pieces into one continuous daughter strand.

modules.description: All major replication fork components are shown together with labels and a summary panel connecting enzyme function to leading-lagging asymmetry.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify helicase, SSBs, leading-strand polymerase, lagging-strand polymerase, and ligase in one replication fork.
Summarize the function of each major replication protein.
Connect antiparallel DNA structure and 5'-to-3' polymerase activity to replication asymmetry.
instructions: Inspect the complete fork and read each component label.
Use the summary panel to match enzymes with their roles.
Focus on how opposite template directions cause leading and lagging synthesis.

components.text: Helicase: unwinds
SSBs: stabilize
Leading polymerase: continuous
Lagging polymerase: fragments
Ligase: seals
Replication fork summary

clips.changeMeaning: The complete replication fork appears with all major component labels, consolidating the separate replication mechanisms into a single view.
clips.narration: Here all replication fork components are working together: helicase opens DNA, SSBs stabilize templates, polymerases synthesize new strands, and ligase seals lagging-strand fragments.

components.text: Helicase opens | SSBs stabilize | Polymerase builds | Ligase seals

clips.changeMeaning: A compact summary panel appears below the model to reinforce each enzyme function after students see the labeled spatial arrangement.
clips.narration: Each protein performs a specific task, but replication succeeds because these activities are coordinated at the fork.

components.text: Antiparallel templates + 5'→3' polymerase = leading/lagging asymmetry

clips.changeMeaning: The summary text changes to emphasize the causal conceptual link between antiparallel templates and asymmetric leading versus lagging synthesis.
clips.narration: The central concept is that structure dictates mechanism. Because the templates are antiparallel and polymerase builds only 5 prime to 3 prime, one daughter strand is leading and the other is lagging.

modules.description: Gold parental strands and silver new strands are tracked through one and two rounds of replication, with a prediction prompt before the second round result.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Define semiconservative replication as conserving one parental strand in each daughter after one round.
Predict the composition of molecules after a second round of replication.
Use strand colors to reason through template-based inheritance.
instructions: Gold marks original parental strands; silver marks newly synthesized strands.
Observe round one, then choose the predicted round-two outcome mentally before the reveal.
Compare your prediction with the final four molecules.

components.text: Predict round 2: A) all hybrid  B) 2 hybrid + 2 silver  C) all silver
Gold = original parental strands; silver = newly synthesized strands

clips.changeMeaning: A fully gold parental DNA molecule establishes the color code for original strands before replication outcomes are shown.
clips.narration: Gold marks the original parental DNA strands. We will follow these strands to understand why replication is called semiconservative.

components.text: Round 1: each daughter has 1 gold parental + 1 silver new strand

clips.changeMeaning: The parental molecule is replaced by two hybrid daughter molecules, showing that each daughter contains one old and one newly synthesized strand.
clips.narration: After one round, each daughter molecule has one gold parental strand and one silver newly synthesized strand. Each daughter conserves half of the parental molecule.

components.text: Predict the four molecules produced by a second round

clips.changeMeaning: A prediction panel appears beneath the round-one daughters, asking students to reason about the second round before seeing the result.
clips.narration: Now predict what happens after a second round. Will all four molecules be hybrid, will two be hybrid and two fully silver, or will all four be fully silver?

components.text: Round 2 result: 2 hybrid molecules + 2 fully silver molecules

clips.changeMeaning: The prediction panel and two daughter molecules are replaced by a four-molecule result set confirming two hybrid and two fully silver molecules.
clips.narration: The correct result is two hybrid molecules and two fully silver molecules. Original gold strands remain in only two lineages, while silver strands from round one can template fully silver products.

modules.moduleName: Scene 11: DNA Structure and Replication Recap
modules.description: A final summary screen highlights the six major concept areas: helix structure, base pairing, antiparallel directionality, fork enzymes, leading/lagging synthesis, and semiconservative inheritance.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Summarize the main structural features of DNA introduced in the lab.
Connect complementary base pairing and antiparallel directionality to replication mechanics.
Review semiconservative inheritance after one and two replication rounds.
instructions: Read each highlighted recap item as it appears.
Use the final prompt to test whether you can connect DNA structure to replication mechanism.
Replay earlier modules if any concept is unclear.

components.text: DNA Structure and Replication Recap
Core question: how does DNA structure dictate replication mechanism?

1. Double helix: backbones outside, bases inside
2. Pairing: A-T has 2 H bonds; G-C has 3

clips.changeMeaning: The recap panel updates to the first two concept areas and the highlight bar appears, emphasizing the structural basis of DNA and base-pair specificity.
clips.narration: First, DNA is a double helix with sugar-phosphate backbones outside and paired bases inside. Complementary pairing is specific: A with T, and G with C.

components.text:
3. Antiparallel: one 5'→3', one 3'→5'
4. Fork proteins: helicase, SSBs, polymerase, ligase

clips.changeMeaning: The recap panel changes to antiparallel directionality and enzyme roles, connecting DNA structure with the components operating at the fork.
clips.narration: Second, the strands are antiparallel because their backbones have opposite chemical directions. At the fork, helicase, SSBs, polymerase, and ligase perform coordinated jobs.

components.text:
5. Leading continuous; lagging uses Okazaki fragments
6. Semiconservative: each daughter keeps one template strand
Antiparallel DNA + 5'→3' polymerase activity shapes replication

clips.changeMeaning: The final recap emphasizes leading-lagging asymmetry and semiconservative inheritance, tying the lab's structural and mechanistic themes together.
clips.narration: Finally, leading and lagging strands arise from antiparallel templates and one-way polymerase activity. Replication is semiconservative because each daughter molecule preserves one parental template strand.
